items.title: Small Models, Big Results: Training a Finance Agent for Under $500 — Charles Dickens, Snorkel AI
items.description:
A 4 billion parameter model, trained with RL for under $500, beat its 235 billion parameter sibling on real financial questions.

Charles Dickens, research scientist at Snorkel AI, shares how Snorkel and UC Berkeley's Sky Computing Lab trained a small model to beat a much bigger one. Working from SEC 10-K filings, they built FinQA, a financial question-answering dataset with expert-validated answers, and found even frontier models hallucinating table schemas, flooding their own context, and repeating failed strategies. Using the open-source rLLM framework and reinforcement learning with a simple pass/fail reward, they trained a Qwen3 4B model for under $500 that reached about 60% versus 51% for the 235B model. The skills transferred to harder multi-table questions without hurting general tool use. Surprisingly, simpler training data and simpler rewards worked best, because the real bottleneck was disciplined tool use, not reasoning depth.

In this talk:
• How the FinQA dataset was built and verified from 10-K filings
• Failure modes: hallucinated schemas, context flooding, poor recovery
• Training a 4B model with RL in rLLM for under $500
• Why simple data and binary rewards beat fancier setups

Why Your Company Needs a Context Graph (and How to Build It) — Gil Feig, Merge
items.description:
Your agent can tell you why one customer was upset. Ask which customers were upset last year, and it falls apart.

Gil Feig, co-founder and CTO of Merge, explains why every company needs a context graph, a company brain that brings together third-party data, structured context, memories and skills. Using the question "which customers were upset last week?", he shows why connecting a few MCP servers isn't enough: live API lookups can't search across large datasets, so you need a synced copy for semantic queries, alongside live calls for simple lookups. He walks through the architecture: a router, synced and live context, a summarizer, and skills and memory that encode how your company actually defines things like a happy customer. He covers four tiers of context including derived summaries, a decision flowchart for when to use cache or live data, and why every answer must keep track of where its data came from.

In this talk:
• Why MCP live lookups can't answer questions across large datasets
• Combining synced data, live lookups, a router and a summarizer
• Why company skills and memory belong in the context layer
• Traceability: where data came from, when, and what invalidates it

items.title: Generation Is Cheap, Review Is Expensive: How to Stop Shipping AI Slop — Gabriel Martinez, G2i
items.description:
Slop isn't AI-written code. It's work that looks finished before the thinking is.

Gabriel "Gabo" Martinez, engineering manager and self-described slop warden at G2i, explains what slop really is: what happens when generation outruns judgment, when ambiguity gets cleared with guesses and nobody notices there was a choice to make. He's not anti-AI, but argues we need to sober up. Code is still a liability, agents make a messy codebase messier faster, and quick prototypes convince stakeholders the hard part is done. He covers the pressure to merge faster than you can review, thousand-line PRs, 20-page AI docs that push the thinking onto reviewers, and why generation is cheap but evaluation is expensive. His fixes are conventions, diagrams as the review surface, small reviewable changes and clear ownership, inspired by Rails, plus why G2i built ORC.

In this talk:
• What slop is, and why it's about missing judgment, not AI
• Why code is a liability and AI makes the ball of mud bigger
• Incentives that push teams to merge faster than they can review
• Conventions, diagrams and small changes that keep humans in control

items.title: From Context to Memory: Your Agents Need a Real Memory Layer — Anders Swanson, Oracle
items.description:
Your agent rereads the same files every session because nothing it learned was saved.

Anders Swanson, developer evangelist for Oracle Database, treats agent memory as a systems problem. Context windows aren't memory, bigger windows aren't the fix, and markdown scratch pads and grep don't scale. Keep going down that road and you'll end up building your own database. He walks through the pattern modern memory systems are converging on: formation, recall, evolution and evaluation, plus governance. That means typed memories (episodic, semantic, procedural and working state), a storage schema with vectors, text indexes, graph links, time and audit history, redaction before anything is written, and hybrid search that blends several retrieval methods. He covers failure modes like stale, mis-scoped, poisoned and conflicting memories, and why feedback is what closes the loop.

In this talk:
• Why context windows and scratch files aren't memory
• Typed memories and a storage schema built for recall
• Forming memories safely, and recalling them with hybrid search
• Stale, poisoned and conflicting memories, and how feedback fixes them

items.title: Designing CLIs for Agents, Not Humans — Pedro Lopez, Airbyte
items.description:
Airbyte built both an MCP server and a CLI so agents can use its data. Here's what each one is actually good for.

Pedro Lopez, software engineer at Airbyte, shares lessons from building two ways for AI agents to reach company data through Airbyte's Context Store, a search-optimized index of tools like Zendesk, Stripe and HubSpot. Both are thin interfaces over one platform, built from OpenAPI specs. For the MCP server, he explains why to keep the tool count small and use progressive discovery, why OAuth is the only realistic way to sign in, why users expect long-lived sessions, and why URL elicitation isn't ready across clients yet. For the CLI, he explains designing for agents instead of humans: JSON in and JSON out, consistent noun-verb commands, skills that ship with the tool, and no interactive prompts. He closes with when to choose MCP and when to choose a CLI.

In this talk:
• Keeping MCP tool counts small with progressive discovery
• OAuth, long sessions, and elicitation in real MCP clients
• Designing a CLI for agents: JSON in, JSON out, consistency, skills
• When to choose MCP, and when to choose a CLI

items.title: RustConf 2025 Interview: Manish Goregaokar, Rust Devtools
items.description:
At RustConf 2025 in Seattle, the Rust Project Content Team talks with Manish Goregaokar: Clippy co-creator, Servo alum, and around eleven years in the Rust Project, now working on internationalization with ICU4X and interop tooling with Diplomat.

Manish shares how contributing to Servo in 2013-2014, when nightly Rust broke every few weeks, pulled him from working with Rust into working on Rust, and how a silly project full of lints became Clippy. Topics include:

• Clippy's origins and the culture of mentorship inherited from Servo: writing lints as an accessible on-ramp to compiler internals
• How the Rust community changed from one tight-knit group into many overlapping worlds, and why that's healthy
• The surprise of 1.0: the flood of Python and JavaScript developers who were always interested in systems programming once the barrier came down
• An ontology of interop tooling: unidirectional versus bidirectional tools, and why "other languages calling Rust libraries" was the underserved direction
• Diplomat: bridge modules generating a C API, a typed AST, and independently developed backends for C, C++, JavaScript/Wasm, Dart, Kotlin, Java, and Python
• ICU4X: internationalization designed from scratch to be modular, embedded-friendly, and pluggable about data, so your app doesn't mispluralize Polish
• Restraint about writing crates de novo, nerd-sniping yourself, and designs like ZeroVec and Yoke that others had to convince him to build
• jj (Jujutsu): a Rust version control system with changes as first-class concepts distinct from commits

items.title: Building on the Codex Harness — Dominik Kundel, OpenAI
items.description:
Building your own agent harness is daunting. So use the one that already powers Codex.

Dominik Kundel from OpenAI's Codex developer experience team explains the Codex App Server, the open-source JSON-RPC protocol that wraps the Codex harness and powers the Codex app, the IDE extensions, and third-party clients in Xcode, JetBrains and more. Using an inspector he built, he shows the real events flowing between the Codex app and the server, then covers what you can control: more than 120 client messages, sign in with ChatGPT so users bring their own subscription, developer instructions layered on top of the system prompt, dynamic and deferred tools, and per-thread model and sandbox settings. He explains how to ship the binary, generate bindings, and use the Python SDK, when to use codex exec instead, and demos Codex running inside Doom.

In this talk:
• What the Codex App Server is, and how it compares to ACP
• Customizing the agent with developer instructions and deferred dynamic tools
• Shipping the binary, generating bindings, and the Python SDK

items.title: Stop Prompting — Greg Pstrucha, Sentry
items.description:
You correct your agent. It says "You're absolutely right." Five minutes later, after compaction, it makes the same mistake again.

Greg Pstrucha, who works on the infrastructure behind Seer, Sentry's debugging agent, argues you should stop re-prompting your coding agent and start codifying the rules you keep repeating. Agents have no memory, so the same elementary mistakes come back: overly defensive code, useless tests, endpoints nobody needs. Tests, strict types and especially linters turn those corrections into deterministic checks, and with agents, writing a custom lint rule is now cheap. He shows real examples from Sentry: lint rules that keep endpoints in sync with the OpenAPI schema, and a long game of whack-a-mole to keep agent skills accurate. For qualitative judgment, he uses written policies and a "Grumpy Engineer" review loop, and warns that agents will game any number you hand them, like test coverage.

In this talk:
• Why re-prompting fails, and why lint rules are now cheap to write
• Mining your transcripts and PR reviews for rules worth enforcing
• Examples from Sentry: API schema checks and linting agent skills
• Policies and review agents for what linters can't catch, and why metrics get gamed

DESCRIPTION
Garrison Hinson-Hasty, author of “Systems Programming with Zig” and a contributor to the Zig compiler, joins Trevor Berrange Sanchez to explain why he wrote a book on a pre-1.0 language that breaks frequently (he's currently updating the last seven chapters for Zig 0.16). His answer: the language's slow march toward 1.0 is a feature, and learning it now teaches you why its decisions stick. The conversation's core thesis is that Zig is countercultural: instead of stacking new abstractions on old ones, it reuses well-tested ideas and "never adds too much”. "Simple", in the Zig community's sense, means simple relative to what the machine is doing, with integer and pointer types that map closely to how you'd think about data in assembly. Chapter 6's CHIP-8 interpreter shows this: a few integers, some buffers, and elegant results. The same philosophy explains Zig's missing string type. Strings are just byte sequences with a length, and the language leaves encoding choices to you. Garrison notes that Rust, by contrast, now has to maintain its many string types forever.

Two practical takeaways for working engineers. First, allocators: because Zig encourages flat, data-oriented design, the book barely needs dynamic allocation, and when it does, allocators let you reason about memory for a whole phase of a program (say, a compiler's parser) as one unit rather than tracking the lifetime of every AST node. items.description:
Trace redaction permanently removes sensitive data from your traces, for when something like an API key ends up in a span attribute. Tempo 3.0 could do it, but only from a list of trace IDs, so you had to go find every affected trace first. In Tempo 3.1 you can hand it a TraceQL query instead.

items.title: AI Writes More PRs. Who Validates Them? — Ali-Reza Adl-Tabatabai, Sonar
items.description:
AI means more PRs, bigger PRs, and more bugs. Your choice is to slow down or rubber-stamp, unless validation gets automated too.

Ali-Reza Adl-Tabatabai, co-founder of Gitar (now part of Sonar), focuses on verifying code. CI and code review are where quality gates live, and they get slower and more expensive as teams grow. AI makes it worse with more and bigger PRs, leaving teams to either slow down or rubber-stamp and risk incidents. His answer is agentic validation: an agent that reviews PRs with as little noise as possible, explains CI failures and catches flaky tests, fixes issues until the PR is green, and approves and merges based on rules you set. He describes how users build trust step by step toward full automation, the insights it gives platform teams and leaders, what's under the hood (control plane, custom harness and LLM proxy), and why combining agents with program analysis in SonarQube beats either alone.

In this talk:
• Why AI-generated code turns CI and code review into a bottleneck
• Agentic validation: review, CI analysis, autofix and auto-merge

items.title: Why 80% Reliability Isn't Good Enough — Felipe Blanes, Amazon AGI Lab
items.description:
Your agent scores great on benchmarks. Then real customers use it and it breaks.

Felipe Blanes from the Amazon AGI Lab shares what he learned working directly with customers of Nova Act, Amazon's service for building browser agents, from research preview to general availability on AWS. He calls the core problem the benchmark illusion: static evals look great until customers do things nobody expected, and then all you have left is hope. His fix is an eval flywheel built around the customer: define success the way the customer does, capture signals (including by talking to customers), diagnose gaps in the model, harness or product, and feed them into decisions. He explains the trust cliff (80% reliability feels like more work; around 92% feels trustworthy), why being open about limits builds more trust than higher benchmarks, surprising use cases from Amazon Leo, Hertz and Sola, and four principles for keeping evals fresh.

In this talk:
• The benchmark illusion, and why static evals leave you hoping
• A four-step eval flywheel driven by real customer signals
• The trust cliff: why 80% reliability isn't enough
• Why being open about limits builds more trust than higher scores

items.title: Brains vs Hands: How to Run AI Agents Safely in Production — Viren Baraiya
items.description:
Let the model decide what should happen next. Never let it improvise how a production cluster gets restarted.

Viren Baraiya, co-founder and CTO of Orkes and the original creator of Netflix Conductor, explains how to run agents in production. Real agents aren't just chatbots: they run on schedules, react to events, coordinate other agents and can run for months, so the harness around them starts to look like an application, much like a set of microservices. His key idea is a clean split between the brain and the hands. The LLM plans what should happen next; a deterministic, durable harness does the actual work, with approval gates, idempotent steps and recorded side effects. He frames agent harnesses as late-bound sagas, workflows the agent assembles at runtime, and demos an SRE agent whose plan is compiled into a Conductor workflow, executed, checked and re-planned over two loops.

In this talk:
• Background, scheduled, event-driven and long-running agents
• Why the harness is the application, mixing deterministic and non-deterministic parts
• The brain and the hands: the LLM plans, the harness executes
• Demo: an SRE agent's plan compiled into a durable workflow

Coding agents are great inside one repo. Postman has 115 microservices and thousands of endpoints.

Kamalakannan Nandagopal, staff engineer at Postman, shares how Postman made coding agents work across a real distributed system. Borrowing from Postman's go-to-market team, they realized APIs are the context layer, and built an API context graph that maps every service, endpoint, implementation and call, all the way down to databases, with every data point grounded in code or production telemetry. In this talk:
• Why coding agents struggle with distributed systems and microservices

items.title: Turning Agent Memory Into Skills That Work — Will Lyon, Neo4j
items.description:
Agents finish a task, then forget what they learned. Retrieval alone won't fix that.

Will Lyon, senior product manager at Neo4j, explains why agent memory built on embeddings and retrieval isn't enough: recall isn't actionable knowledge. Agents need knowledge that is connected, typed and traceable. He shows Neo4j's model of agent memory as a context graph with short-term, long-term and reasoning memory, covering entity extraction and resolution, shared ontologies, and decision traces that let many agents learn from each other. Then he turns memory into action: distilling grounded, governed skills from the graph, based on Neo4j research that treats skills as typed execution graphs, with checks for grounding, coverage and coherence, and alerts when a skill goes stale. He demos the Neo4j Agent Memory Service distilling a patient-intake skill from a healthcare conversation.

In this talk:
• Why retrieval isn't actionable knowledge
• Short-term, long-term and reasoning memory in one context graph
• Distilling grounded, governed skills from memory
• Demo: the Neo4j Agent Memory Service building a skill from a conversation

Your coding agent is fast. But it can't see how your services actually run, so it guesses.

Matt Gibiec, who leads AI-native solutions engineering at Dynatrace, explains why AI agents need something like a nervous system: real context from the environment they're changing. Agents get stuck in loops, cause operational and security issues, and are hard to measure, because they work fast but blind, only as good as the data they can see. He introduces Bluebox by Dynatrace, an observability agent for your coding agent, and walks through scenarios: bringing production dependencies into local testing so a change that works on your laptop doesn't break three other services, spotting issues before users feel them, suggesting fixes that account for the rest of the system, and briefing agents with real usage data before they build, with a human keeping final control.

In this talk:
• Why agents loop, hallucinate and break things without environment context
• Bringing production dependencies into local testing

• Planning before you prompt, with a human approving the final fix

items.title: Why We Deleted Our MCP Server and Rebuilt It — Abhi Arya, Reducto
items.description:
Reducto gave its whole team an MCP server with a tool for every endpoint. It broke the same day.

Abhi Arya, who works on product at Reducto, argues that building agent-first software comes down to one question: who pays when the agent is wrong? He describes three approaches, auto mode, user-first, and agent experience in service of the user, and how Reducto learned the difference. A first MCP server with one tool per API endpoint demoed well but fell apart when the whole team used it: the agent built entire workflows confidently, and nobody could explain them. He deleted it in one commit and rebuilt with fewer tools that carry the structure of real work, plus a snapshot tool for live state. Then he made uncertainty visible, with confidence scores and an agent that asks instead of guessing, and added instrumentation that made the system improve on its own, until the sales team adopted it without being asked.

In this talk:
• Auto mode vs user-first vs agent experience in service of the user
• Why one tool per API endpoint fails, and what to build instead
• Making uncertainty visible: confidence scores and asking instead of guessing
• Instrumentation that turns usage into a self-improving loop

items.title: AI Just Broke the #1 Rule of Software Engineering
items.description:
Decades of software management taught us one rule: developers will always have more work than time.
AI velocity just broke that rule.

Teams are now moving so fast they’re outpacing their pipelines - and running out of qualified work to build.

🔗 Watch Hannah Foxwell’s full talk: https://bit.ly/4B0vqfu 

#SoftwareEngineering #DeveloperTools #TechLeadership #InfoQ #AICoding #EngineeringManagement
